extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, court staff, and practitioners managing patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical judicial guidance for early case management of patent litigation, including jurisdiction, venue, transfer motions, scheduling, coordination of multiple cases, and checklists for issues that affect cost, complexity, and early resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal jurisdiction and jurisdictional discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Given uncertainty surrounding the “stream of commerce” test, courts should emphasize jurisdictional discovery where the existing record is inadequate to determine personal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stream-of-commerce tests leave uncertainty, vacate dismissals and remand for jurisdictional discovery (e.g., Trintec Indus. v. Pedre; Commissariat a l’Energie Atomique v. Chi Mei). Courts have denied dismissal and ordered jurisdictional discovery where allegations can be supplemented; district courts can order jurisdictional discovery rather than decide on an incomplete record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original subject-matter jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. §1338(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal district courts have exclusive original jurisdiction of 'any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents.' Whether a claim 'arises under' is determined by the well-pleaded complaint rule and by the complaint alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Christianson v. Colt Industries and Holmes Group principles: if the plaintiff’s complaint on its face presents a federal patent issue, the case arises under federal patent law. Determine patent jurisdiction solely on the basis of the complaint, not counterclaims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental jurisdiction for related state-law claims (28 U.S.C. §1367)
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims that form part of the same Article III case or controversy, but supplemental claims must be dismissed if there is no underlying original jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff lacks standing to bring federal claims, supplemental state-law claims must be dismissed (Textile Prods. v. Mead). District courts have discretionary authority under §1367(c) to retain or dismiss supplemental claims even after federal claims are dismissed on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for patent cases (28 U.S.C. §1391)
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue is generally proper in any district in which infringing activity (broadly defined as making, selling, or offering for sale) has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs may file where infringing activity occurred; defendants often respond with motions to transfer venue if they lack physical presence in that district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue transfer legal standard (28 U.S.C. §1404(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may transfer any civil action to another district for the convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice; transfer motions should be promptly decided and are evaluated based on the situation when suit was instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Hoffman v. Blaski: decide transfers based on the facts at filing. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 72(a) requires prompt handling. In re EMC Corp. stresses addressing transfer motions at the outset. Norwood v. Kirkpatrick directs courts to apply §1404(a) as written, without forum non conveniens constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer analysis — private convenience factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding a §1404(a) motion, balance private convenience factors including access to sources of proof, availability of compulsory process, cost for willing witnesses, and other practical problems affecting ease, expedition, and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re TS Tech USA Corp. lists these convenience factors. Courts should weigh where documentary evidence and witnesses are located and whether compulsory process is available to secure their attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer analysis — public interest factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-interest considerations include court congestion, local interest in deciding local issues, forum familiarity with governing law, and avoidance of conflict-of-law problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply public factors alongside private ones (In re TS Tech). Courts balance these to determine whether transferee venue is clearly more convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to plaintiff’s forum choice and the 'good cause' burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff’s chosen forum is entitled to deference; the moving party must show good cause to overcome that deference — i.e., that the transferee venue is 'clearly more convenient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fifth Circuit en banc in In re Volkswagen articulated that 'good cause' requires satisfying statutory requirements and clearly demonstrating transfer is for convenience and justice. The plaintiff’s forum choice is reflected in the movant’s burden rather than as an independent factor (Volkswagen, 545 F.3d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and prompt resolution of transfer motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer motions should be addressed early in litigation and decided promptly; familiarity gained by the district court with the litigation after filing is irrelevant to the transfer analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re EMC and In re Google demonstrate the importance of timely resolution — courts have been directed to stay proceedings and decide aged transfer motions. Transfer is judged by the circumstances at the time suit was filed (Hoffman v. Blaski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus relief for patently erroneous denials of transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit may grant a writ of mandamus to correct a patently erroneous denial of transfer in extraordinary situations showing clear abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where mandamus was granted include In re Acer, In re Nintendo, In re Microsoft, In re Zimmer Holdings, and In re TS Tech — typically where most witnesses and evidence are closer to the transferee venue and few convenience factors favor the transferor venue. Mandamus is discretionary and applied in extraordinary situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts that, standing alone, are insufficient to maintain venue
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of factual showings that courts have held insufficient, by themselves, to justify retaining venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2.4 enumerates examples: (1) deference to plaintiff’s choice of forum; (2) presence of electronic documents in the forum; (3) plaintiff’s presence solely for litigation (e.g., incorporating days before filing; sharing office space to create venue); (4) past experience of transferee forum with the patent; (5) defendant sells allegedly infringing products in the forum; (6) 'central location' rationale between witnesses and documents; (7) defendant incorporated in forum but maintains no other business presence. Courts have rejected these, without more, as sufficient to maintain venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing multiple patent cases and multidistrict coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for managing multiple patent cases include consolidation/coordination in a single district, transfer under §1404(a), or JPML centralization under §1407 for pretrial proceedings when convenient and efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPML may centralize patent cases for pretrial proceedings to promote judicial economy (e.g., In re Laughlin Prods.; In re Bear Creek). When consolidation is not possible, courts can designate a lead case, stay related matters, conduct joint hearings, appoint special masters under Fed. R. Civ. P. 53, require joint discovery plans, and use protective orders to share discovery across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling order content for patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheduling orders in patent cases should include dates and deadlines tailored to patent-specific issues to balance efficiency with adequate development of technical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended scheduling order items include: last date to disclose intention to rely on advice of counsel as a defense; last date to add inequitable conduct allegations without leave; disclosure of invalidity and infringement contentions; close of fact discovery; claim-construction hearing date; close of expert discovery; last date for filing and hearing dispositive motions; schedule for Daubert motions; possibility of staggering expert report deadlines with damages reports due before technical reports; requiring substantial disclosure of damages theories in initial disclosures; and setting an early date for motions to dismiss to narrow the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-management conference best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial Rule 26(f)/Rule 16(b) case-management conferences should identify substantive and business issues, establish ground rules for cooperation, and set expectations for pacing and disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conferences may be held off the record for informality, or on the record for particularly complex/contentious cases. Courts often issue a standing order or brief 'advisory' document addressing special aspects of patent litigation and expectations; courts may require lead counsel to provide that advisory to clients. Use the conference to solicit a proposed calendar in the Rule 26(f) Joint Case Management Statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and market considerations checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess market and business facts that affect damages, injunctive relief, settlement prospects, and case management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant questions: What are the accused products? Do they encompass the accused infringer’s entire business or are they part of a larger line? Market size (approximate annual sales)? Does plaintiff make a competing product? Are there other competitors? Prior business relationship between parties? Financial state of the parties (profits, projections)? Are the parties public companies? How much time remains before asserted patents expire? Implications include effects on damages, willingness to litigate to trial, injunctive relief considerations, and potential for business-destroying judgments favoring stays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive considerations checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify substantive legal and technical issues that affect case complexity and opportunities for early resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues to address: Is the asserting party the named inventor or how were rights acquired? Is there parallel litigation (ITC) or PTAB review? Is there a dispute about structure/function of the accused device? Is technology complex? Are there substantive issues amenable to early resolution (e.g., dispositive claim terms, patent eligibility)? Have asserted patents been litigated or licensed before? Are patents connected to industry standards or subject to FRAND obligations? Have patents been reexamined at the USPTO? Will opinion-of-counsel waiver issues arise? Has litigation counsel been involved in prosecution? Discuss expert witness role limitations and proof plans for indirect infringement, damages theories (reasonable royalty, entire-market-value rule), and whether surveys will be used — all to guide discovery and trial preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing cooperation and potential for early resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage early cooperation on discovery scope, electronic discovery, claim-construction scope, and dispute-limitation mechanisms to promote efficiency and early settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss and consider limits on depositions, document requests, requests for admission, and interrogatories (modifying the 25-interrogatory limit if needed). Address electronic discovery issues early, consider limiting number of claim terms to be construed, require meet-and-confer before bringing discovery disputes, limit discovery disputes requiring court intervention, consider adopting or adapting patent local rules, and plan timing of summary judgment relative to claim construction. Consider mediation early and appoint mediator or initiate selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing multidefendant litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: At an early stage, identify the patentee’s basis for suing multiple defendants to better manage joinder, discovery scope, and case complexity under the AIA and relevant Federal Circuit precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multidefendant suits may be efficient for plaintiffs but can raise joinder issues when accused conduct or products differ across defendants (see In re EMC Corp.). The court should identify reasons for including multiple defendants early and tailor management accordingly (e.g., lead cases, bifurcated discovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidefendant cases based on standards compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleged infringement stems from compliance with an industry standard, multiple manufacturers may be accused, and discovery can be limited if infringement is based purely on practicing mandatory standard features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If practice of a mandatory feature of a standard is the sole asserted infringing activity, discovery regarding functional specifications of the accused products can often be fairly limited. Identifying standards-based accusations early improves case management and narrow discovery.
